why: We use it for the character of a village water point rather than for any measurement: that one source served drinking, cooking and washing, and that the place where water was drawn was also where villagers stopped to talk - which is why a well on our maps is drawn as somewhere people gather and not as plumbing. It is a short institutional piece written with the village's own preservation committee to introduce the place to foreign readers; Harie is also unusual in having spring water at every door, which most villages did not.

We use it for a date rather than a measurement: it places the neat rectangular grid of Japanese paddy in the Meiji era and after, which is why the fields on our maps keep the irregular shapes the ground gave them. What we take is an institution and its statute, which is the kind of thing such an article states plainly.

We use it to date the practice, because it tells us straight-row planting was rare before Meiji and was promoted nationally through the 1890s and 1900s together with the hand-pushed inter-row weeder (田打車), planting ropes and rulers, which is why our paddies are not drawn as tidy grids of aligned seedlings. Because it is written about a Meiji reform, what it tells us about earlier practice comes by contrast rather than by direct description.

We use its rule of thumb - one koku as an adult's rice for a year - to turn a settlement's assessed yield into a number of mouths it could feed, and the article supplies its own hedge, that a standard stipend ran nearer 1.8 koku of brown rice, which keeps the round figure from being treated as exact. The koku equivalence is in any case a convention of assessment rather than a measured diet.

It gives the nominal tax rate in the words of five published reference works, which is what our rent and yield arithmetic starts from. Its limits are that the rate is a nominal one, and the sources themselves say the real burden varied with soil, harvest and region; and that one of them hedges the very transition we quote - the shift to five-five after the Kyoho era is "said to have" happened "but is not certain" - so the later rate is a convention rather than a settled fact.

It gives the definition of the managed belt between village and mountain, the mosaic of land uses in it, and two practices our maps draw - leaf litter gathered for the paddies and the coppice cut on a cycle. Its limits are that it is flagged as still being translated from the Japanese article; that the one Edo-period statement we lean on, the leaf gathering, carries no citation in the article; that the fifteen-to-twenty-year cutting cycle is stated in the present tense and cited to a 2017 ecology paper about present-day management, so a premodern rotation is being read from a modern study of a traditional practice; and that the word itself is largely a twentieth-century coinage, which is our knowledge rather than the page's.

It answers, for a city map, where the poor were buried and what that ground looked like: bad land, deliberately walled off, laid out in numbered rows rather than left as an open field. It describes a Chinese institution, which suits the imperial-Chinese half of our setting more directly than the Japanese half; we take from it the siting and the layout, which its own sources support, rather than any count.

We use it for one point about form rather than any number: that the extent of such a field had no clear definition, which is our warrant for drawing a burial ground as an unbounded stretch of hillside rather than a walled or fenced plot. It describes the capital's own enormous burial fields, so it tells us the shape of the thing and never the scale a village graveyard should have.

It tells us that the gates are donations and roughly how thickly the most heavily endowed shrine in the country came to be lined with them, which is the upper bound a map needs when it draws a shrine approach. Its limits are that the count is a present-day round number accumulated since the Edo period, not a period census, and only the whole-mountain figure is readable on the site, so any density per stretch of path is derived by us; and that this is the most famous shrine of its kind, so it is a ceiling and never a typical case.

It is the shrine's own dating of the donated-gate custom to the Edo period, which is what lets a premodern map draw a votive approach at all rather than a modern tourist one. Its limits are the same as its sibling's: the most famous shrine of its kind, so it bounds the top of the range and never the middle.

The article counts eight torii along the approach and gives no distances between them, so no spacing figure on our maps comes from it. It describes a modern shrine of exceptional scale, which makes it a poor model for the small country shrines our settlements mostly carry.

Deciding how many monks a settlement of a given size can hold needs an order of magnitude for the share of a population living in religious orders, and this supplies one attributed to a dynastic record - under half a percent. The limits are real: a Song Chinese count is standing in for the whole setting; and an imperial count is a count of registered clergy, which is not the same as everyone living in a temple.

It is straightforward evidence for something our maps get wrong by default, that a real river is not one name from source to sea but a chain of local names, each belonging to the stretch the people beside it know. It describes one enormous continental river in modern usage, so we take the naming habit from it as a principle and not the names or the reach lengths as anything to scale from.

It supports a small point of naming that our maps follow, that one river can legitimately carry different names along its course, so a river labeled one thing at a settlement need not be labeled the same thing upstream. It is about a single modern river, used only for a naming convention it states plainly, and nothing on any map depends on a number from it.

It is cited for a small point of naming that matters on a map: one river can carry different names along different reaches and in different mouths, so a watercourse crossing a city need not be labeled the same at both ends. It is about one specific river in one city; we use it as an example of the naming habit rather than as evidence about any other river, and where it does not confirm a name we have seen elsewhere we do not claim it.

We use it for why a narrow valley floor makes easily worked paddy once it drains, and for the common rights villagers held over the neighboring woods, which is what puts a firewood wood on the slope beside a valley-bottom field on our maps. It speaks for eastern Japan in particular; and carrying those common rights on from firewood to a reed bed is a step our own record takes, not something the article says.

It is a plain, well referenced account of a castle whose defense was its marsh rather than its stonework, which is exactly the question our wet defensive belt asks: whether low wetland was treated as a work of fortification and not merely as bad ground. The flooding is a single spectacular siege rather than routine practice; and it tells us that a wet belt was defensively real, not how wide an ordinary one was.

Our maps draw the worn tracks between a farmhouse, its yard and its fields, and this tells us how little traffic it takes to make one visible and what line it follows around a slope or an obstacle, which is exactly the rule we needed. Its limits are that the fifteen-passage figure comes from a modern wilderness-recreation handbook about soft ground in American backcountry rather than from any study of a premodern farmyard, so we use it as an order of magnitude and not as a threshold.

It corroborates the reading that a path is where feet have found the shortest or easiest line - a mechanism of walking that is not bound to a period - which is the only thing we take from it. Its limits are that it supplies none of our distances; and that the one number the record quotes from it, that a path forms after about fifteen crossings, is given there without attribution, so the number's anchor is the 1988 study the record names separately, not the magazine.

One sentence in it, describing prehistoric Korean paddies laid out as squares and rectangles separated by bunds about 10 cm high, is where the height of the low earth walls our maps draw between plots comes from. Its limits are of place: the example is Korean and very early rather than Japanese, cited because it is a readable public statement of a bund height and because a bund's height is set by how deep a flooded plot is held, which varies little across the rice-growing world.

It describes the dispersed-farmstead country of the Tonami plain - thousands of farmhouses each standing in its own fields inside its own grove, and what the grove did for the house - which is the pattern one of our settlement forms is drawn from. Its limits are that it is one plain in one prefecture; and that the density our text gives, about thirty farmsteads to the square kilometer, is our own division of its two round figures and not a number the page states.

We use it for that three-layer profile, which is how we draw the boundary between woodland and cultivated ground as a graded edge rather than a hard line. It is also describing central European woodland, and it was consulted because the English-language article on woodland edges did not carry the layer terms - the layering is a general property of a sunlit forest margin, but the species that would fill each layer in East Asia are not taken from here.

It gives a real case of a village laid out on long strip lots from a road, which is the form one of our settlement types is drawn in. Its limits are that it is lightly sourced on the point we use; that this was a planned, state-subsidized reclamation after a fire, a deliberate special case rather than a village that grew; that it was dry field only, so it carries nothing about a paddy village's form; and that the article says nothing about where the houses stood on the strips - the house at the road end with its fields behind is our placement, drawn from elsewhere, as are the woodlots.

It gives the species of a homestead grove and what each was cut for - the cedar core, the asunaro, zelkova, oak, bamboo, persimmon and chestnut around it, leaves and dead wood for fuel, bamboo for the household's gear - which is what our grove is planted with. Its limits are that it is a conservation council's site rather than a survey; and that the passage we quote is on its regional-comparison page and describes another prefecture's groves - the kainyo of Tonami in Toyama - so it is one municipal body's secondhand description of another region, which happens to agree with the Toyama sources cited beside it.

It is the page that says a red pine is often planted for gardens and windbreaks, which is the human use a map draws rather than the botany. Its limits are that it describes the tree in one Japanese locality.

The landform does not change with the century, so a modern description of it serves a premodern map directly, and we use it for what lies behind a river's bank - wet ground, traditionally worked as paddy, extended over time by draining marsh - which decides where our fields and our houses go on a floodplain.

We use it for one narrow thing: that carrying one channel under another was a real method in old Japanese waterways, and not a modern trick we invented for a map. We take from it only the existence of the technique and the named historical works it points to, never a dimension, a gradient or a construction detail - and the examples it gives are large public irrigation projects, which is a bigger class of work than a village would undertake on its own.

We use it to establish the form itself - that when a canal has to cross a valley the answer is a bridge carrying the water, and what such a bridge looks like - which is a piece of furniture our irrigated landscapes need and which readers rarely expect. It does not date its examples, so it tells us the type exists and how it is built and nothing about when any given one was; the named examples are also nineteenth-century or later works, so we draw the form and not their engineering.

This is the backbone of how we plant a farmstead: which sides carry the grove (north and west against the wind, the east left open for the entrance and its ornamental garden), which trees make it up (sugi, matsu, hinoki and keyaki), and the part that turns a fact into a choice - that the Izumo form once enclosed the whole circumference of a house and was later cut back to a hook covering only the north and west, which is why our maps treat a full ring and a two-sided belt as two correct answers rather than one. It gives us forms and species names and not counts or measurements, and the practice is Japanese and regional, the north-and-west rule following a wind that a warmer corner of the setting need not share.

It tells us that cultivated mulberry is trained as a low shrub rather than let grow into the tree it can become, which is why a mulberry plot on our maps is waist-high bushes and not an orchard. Its limits are that it gives no planting density and no cultivated height in figures, so our height and spacing are guesses; and that it states the low-training habit as a present practice without dating it, so its use for a premodern plot is an assumption the page does not itself carry.

Between them they give the shape of the rice-and-rape year - rape in the paddy over winter, cut in spring before the rice goes in - which is what lets a plot on our maps carry two crops. Their limits are that the calendar we quote is a modern market-garden regime for the vegetable, transplanted at spacing, not the broadcast oilseed stand our maps draw, so its dates are taken as plausible for oilseed rape rather than shown for it; and that the green-manure practice is an explicitly modern Taiwanese one, not an attested premodern rotation.

It gives the rotation this record needs from the Chinese side - rape sown into the paddy after the year's rice is off, so the two never stand together. Its limits are that its worked case is Taiwan, one island of the setting's Chinese half.

We use it for what the building is and where it belongs - a state institution from the early Ming onward, standing in the Confucian temple precinct east of the Dacheng gate rather than inside the magistrate's own compound - which is how we place and label it on a town plan. It describes the Chinese institution, which our setting adapts rather than copies.

It gives the orientation rule our compounds follow - the garden on the south of the formal rooms, beyond the veranda - which fixes the show face of every compound we draw. Its limits are that it is describing an ideal type rather than a surveyed house; that the article carries its editors' own notice that it lacks adequate citations, worth saying when a rule that fixes every compound's face is taken from it; and that it is silent about the north service side, so the kitchen and the servants' quarters rest on other sources.

It gives us the scale and the organization of premodern heavy industry - how a smelting operation was staffed and supplied, and how much iron a large premodern state could make - which is what sizes and sites an ironworking quarter on a town map. Its limits are that the article itself reports that Donald Wagner questions Hartwell's method, so we treat the tonnage as a contested estimate; and a dynasty-wide output figure has to be scaled down hard before it says anything about one town's forges.

We use it for that one climatic fact, because a summer-concentrated rainfall is what makes storage ponds, bunds and flood channels worth drawing in a dry-looking landscape. It covers one region of northern China, not the whole of the country our setting draws on.

This settles a decision every map makes hundreds of times - what an ordinary townsman's roof looked like - by stating that commoners' houses were board-roofed as a general rule throughout the Edo period and that tile only became widespread at its very end, which is why our roofs are boards and thatch and our tile is reserved for temples, gates and the wealthy. We take the direction of the trend rather than any proportion from it, and "the end of the Edo period" is later than the eras our setting draws on, which makes this a reason to draw less tile rather than a license to draw some.

We use it for two things about a walled town: that a Chinese county seat could go unwalled for a long time and then be walled in a hurry under a specific threat, and that such a wall could take a round outline rather than the textbook square. It is about one town in the Yangtze delta, and while the record likes the idea of a wall raised very fast, the article does not put a season on it, so the speed we imply is ours rather than the source's.

We use it for a single fact of placement: the Hyojosho stood at Tatsunokuchi outside Edo Castle, on ground that is now Marunouchi, and not within the castle walls - which is why a capital on our maps puts its high court outside the lord's enceinte. Its limits: it describes one specific Tokugawa institution in one city, which our fictional capitals resemble rather than copy; and it is in Japanese, quoted here in our own translation.

Our capital-tier maps have to show how a very large premodern city was watered, and this gives the whole shape of the answer: an open cut of some forty-three kilometers dropping about ninety meters, run deliberately along the high ground so gravity does the work, then a control point at the city boundary and buried wooden and stone pipes beyond it. It describes one exceptional work built for the shogun's own capital, so it marks the top of what a premodern state could manage rather than ordinary practice; the article also gives no total length for the buried pipe network, so we do not state one.

We use it for how a great castle's approaches were watched - a guardhouse paired with a bridge at each crossing of the moat - and for the conventional round number a place of that size was said to have. Its limits are that the article's own hedge is the point: thirty-six is a traditional figure rather than a count of gates, so we treat it as a convention and not as a total to reproduce.

It gives the dimensions of a great city's moat - 20 m wide, 10 m deep, water all year - which is the top of the range our moats are measured against. Its limits are that this is a former imperial capital, the top of the scale and not a provincial town's ditch; and that the figures describe the moat as it stands today, dredged and landscaped in the modern era - the article dates the wall's construction and rebuilds but gives no period source for the moat's size, so the number is a modern measurement of a much-repaired work rather than a Ming dimension.

It gives one geographic statement our river-and-castle maps use - the Yodo and its tributaries below the northern plateau serving as natural moat and as the water drawn into the castle's moats. Its limits are that the sentence we quote carries no reference in the article, so we take it as well-known geography and nothing more; and that Osaka is the largest castle in Japan, exceptional even for a capital-tier map, so the arrangement transfers and the scale does not.

It gives the 1604 order that made the highway five ken wide, about nine meters, which is the upper bound our trunk roads are measured against. Its limits are that the paragraph we use carries no citation on the page; that the Tokaido was the busiest highway in the country, so its width is a ceiling; and that a decree records what was ordered rather than what was built - the same paragraph reports that the post stations' mandated porters and horses never reached the ordered numbers.

It gives us both the walled ward as a real urban form and the historical bridge that lets a Chinese plan sit under a Japanese-flavored setting, since the Japanese capitals were consciously copied from this one. It describes a planned imperial capital of extraordinary size, so it anchors form and not scale - never a size or a count for the places we draw. Two cautions: the irregular outline it describes is the Han city's, so it says nothing about whether a Tang or later wall was square; and the number of Tang wards is a figure the page gives only as "about 110", which is what our text follows.

It gives the form of an official granary quarter - eight numbered boat channels cut into the river bank with rows of rice storehouses facing them - which is what our granary quays are drawn from. Its limits are that the channel sentence itself carries none; and that this was the shogunal capital's central granary, some 36,000 tsubo with 67 storehouses, an exceptional scale from which only the form transfers to a provincial seat.

It is our type case for the transport canal a city digs for itself - the reason a straight channel runs from a harbor to a construction site and then keeps carrying freight long after the works are done. The attribution of the digging is one the article itself reports as what "is often said" rather than as established, and the Horikawa today is a modern urban waterway, so we take the purpose and the moment of cutting rather than any measurement of it.

It gives the one number the record calls its cleanest case for scaling a service by population - more than six hundred bathhouses in Edo in the early nineteenth century - which is what sets how many bathhouses a city of a given size carries. Its limits are that the sentence we take carries no citation in the article and is written as reported tradition ("it is said there were") rather than as a sourced count; and that Edo was the largest city in Japan at its height, so the step down to a provincial city is ours.
